blocks.text:
Design the core of a professional networking platform like LinkedIn: users send connection requests, the recipient accepts or rejects, and accepted requests form an undirected connection graph. The system must compute the degree of connection between any two users (1st-degree for a direct connection, 2nd-degree through one intermediary, and so on, capped at "3rd or beyond"), and generate a feed of posts authored only by a user's direct (1st-degree) connections, ranked by recency.

  • Actors: User (sends requests, responds, views a feed), NetworkService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: connection request lifecycle, an undirected social graph, BFS-based degree calculation, and 1st-degree-only feed generation.

The distinguishing mechanic is a breadth-first search over an undirected social graph to compute connection degree, the first BFS-shortest-path mechanic in this problem set (Task Management System used DFS for cycle detection on a directed graph; this is a different graph algorithm on a different graph shape).
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Connection requests: a user sends a request to another user; duplicate requests between an already-connected or already-pending pair are rejected.
Responding: the recipient accepts or rejects a pending request; accepting adds an undirected connection edge.
Degree calculation: given any two users, compute their connection degree (1st, 2nd, 3rd-or-beyond) via the shortest path in the connection graph.
Posting: a user can author posts with a timestamp.
Feed generation: for a given user, return posts from their 1st-degree connections only, ranked by recency.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting many users, connections, and posts must not require touching existing request logic.
Extensibility: a different feed ranking policy should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: ranking, notification, and request creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: degree calculation via BFS is capped at 3 hops, keeping it bounded regardless of network size.
Thread safety: two conflicting responses to the same request (accept and reject) submitted concurrently must not both apply.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Is connection degree needed exactly, or is a capped "3rd or beyond" bucket (as real LinkedIn shows) sufficient?
Should the feed include posts from 2nd-degree connections as well, or strictly 1st-degree only?
Can a user cancel their own pending outgoing request before the recipient responds?
Should blocking or removing an existing connection be supported?
Is feed ranking purely recency-based, or should engagement (likes, comments) factor in?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: The connection graph is undirected: once accepted, both users see each other as connections symmetrically.

Degree calculation is capped at a BFS depth of 3; any pair not found within that depth is reported as beyond 3rd-degree, matching how real professional networks summarize distant or disconnected users.
The feed pulls only from 1st-degree connections in this design; 2nd-degree "people you may know"-style suggestions are noted as a future extension, not implemented.
Cancelling a pending outgoing request is out of scope; only the recipient can resolve a pending request (accept or reject).

blocks.text: The design centers on four core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: User, Connection edges, ConnectionRequest, Post

items: User: a member with a set of accepted connection user ids.
ConnectionRequest: a pending, accepted, or rejected request between two users.
Connection: an undirected edge in the social graph, created only when a request is accepted.
Post: content authored by a user with a timestamp, used to build feeds.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: Users connect to each other symmetrically; a user authors many posts; a user sends and receives connection requests

items: User to User (connected) is many-to-many and symmetric.
User to Post is one-to-many.
User to ConnectionRequest is one-to-many in both the sender and recipient roles.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep feed ranking, notification, and request creation decoupled from the core service.
Why needed: how a feed is ordered (recency today, perhaps engagement-weighted tomorrow) is a policy decision that changes independently of how connections and posts are stored.

Why it is the best fit: a new ranking policy is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to NetworkService. What it solves: it isolates a frequently-tuned ranking algorithm from stable orchestration logic.
Why needed: requests sent, accepted, rejected, and duplicate attempts are all events a real networking platform would want to react to (push notifications, email digests).

metadata.alt: NetworkObserver interface notified by NetworkService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: NetworkService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core connection workflow from side effects.
Why needed: request id generation should not be scattered across calling code.
Why it is the best fit: every request is created through one consistent path. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: User: attributes userId, name, connections; responsibility: represent a member and their direct connection set.
ConnectionRequest: attributes requestId, fromUserId, toUserId, status; responsibility: capture one request end-to-end.
ConnectionRequestFactory: method createRequest(fromUserId, toUserId); responsibility: generate sequential request ids.
Post: attributes postId, authorId, content, timestamp; responsibility: represent one piece of authored content.
NetworkService: the orchestrator; responsibility: manage requests, maintain the connection graph, run BFS degree queries, generate feeds, and notify observers.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: FeedRankingStrategy and NetworkObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: FeedRankingStrategy: rank(candidatePosts): returns the posts ordered according to the chosen policy.
NetworkObserver: onConnectionRequestSent / onConnectionAccepted / onConnectionRejected / onDuplicateRequestRejected: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: Three flows below cover a request accepted into a connection, a duplicate request rejected, and a BFS-based degree calculation.

metadata.alt: Alice sends a request to Bob, who accepts it, creating an undirected connection edge
Alice tries to send another request to Bob, who is already a connection
Alice and Carol are not directly connected, but BFS finds Carol at depth 2 through Bob

blocks.text: The end-to-end workflows, alongside their rejection branch, look like this:

metadata.alt: Send request, check for duplicates, respond, add edge on acceptance, query degree via BFS

items: Request path: send request → no existing pending or accepted request between the pair → PENDING.
Duplicate rejection path: send request → already connected or already pending → rejected.
Response path: respond → accepted → undirected edge added, or → rejected → no edge, request closed.
Degree query path: BFS outward from the first user, hop by hop, up to 3 hops, looking for the second user.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: sendConnectionRequest(fromUserId, toUserId): creates a PENDING request, or throws if the pair is already connected or already has a pending request.
respondToRequest(requestId, accept): resolves a PENDING request, adding an edge only on acceptance.
getConnectionDegree(userIdA, userIdB): runs a capped BFS and returns the shortest degree, or a "beyond 3rd" sentinel.
generateFeed(userId): collects posts from 1st-degree connections and returns them ranked by the configured strategy.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: DuplicateConnectionException: a pending or accepted request already exists between the two users.
InvalidRequestException: an unknown request id or unknown user id.
RequestAlreadyRespondedException: respondToRequest is called on a request that is not currently PENDING.

blocks.text: The critical race is two conflicting responses to the same request submitted at nearly the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing to resolve the same request differently; synchronization ensures only the first response applies

blocks.text: Synchronizing the status-check-and-update step per request ensures a request can be resolved exactly once, so it can never end up both accepted and rejected.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new feed ranking policy (engagement-weighted, connection-recency-weighted) is a new FeedRankingStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (push, email) is a new NetworkObserver implementation.
Extending the feed to include 2nd-degree connections is a small change to which posts are gathered before ranking, not a structural change.
"People you may know" suggestions can reuse the same BFS machinery, listing 2nd-degree users not yet directly connected.
Single Responsibility: User tracks its own connection set, FeedRankingStrategy decides ordering, NetworkObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new ranking or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to NetworkService.
Liskov Substitution: any FeedRankingStrategy or NetworkObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: NetworkObserver exposes only the four lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: NetworkService depends on the FeedRankingStrategy and NetworkObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.
getConnectionDegree of a user with itself is a degenerate case that should short-circuit to 0 rather than running BFS.
Two users with no path between them within 3 hops both return the same "beyond 3rd" sentinel, whether they are actually disconnected or just far apart.
generateFeed for a user with zero 1st-degree connections returns an empty list, not an error.
Responding to an already-resolved request throws RequestAlreadyRespondedException rather than silently no-op-ing.
sendConnectionRequest: O(existing requests between the pair) to check for duplicates, effectively O(1) with a lookup keyed by the unordered pair.
getConnectionDegree: O(V + E) bounded by the 3-hop cap, so effectively bounded by the average branching factor cubed rather than the full graph size.
generateFeed: O(1st-degree connections times their post counts) to gather candidates, plus O(n log n) to sort by the ranking strategy.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: User, ConnectionRequest, UserConnection, Post

items: UserConnection is a symmetric join table; a query for a user's connections checks both the userIdA and userIdB columns.
An index on Post(authorId, timestamp) speeds up gathering and ranking a feed.
Extend the feed to optionally include 2nd-degree connections behind a configurable ranking weight.
Add "people you may know" suggestions using the same BFS machinery.
Support cancelling a pending outgoing request.

In a distributed deployment, the BFS-based degree query would need to run against a graph database or a precomputed shortest-path index rather than an in-memory adjacency map, since a live in-memory graph does not scale to a real professional network's size.

NetworkService, including the duplicate-request check, request handling, BFS degree calculation, and feed generation:

codes.python:
# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class DuplicateConnectionException(Exception): pass
class InvalidRequestException(Exception): pass
class RequestAlreadyRespondedException(Exception): pass

# The core orchestrator tying every piece together.
class NetworkService:
    def __init__(self, ranking_strategy):
        self.users = {}          # userId -> User
        self.requests = {}       # requestId -> ConnectionRequest
        self.posts = {}          # authorId -> their posts
        self.ranking_strategy = ranking_strategy  # pluggable ranking policy
        self.observers = []       # listeners
        self.request_counter = 0  # simple id generator

    def add_user(self, user):
        self.users[user.user_id] = user  # register a user
        self.posts[user.user_id] = []      # init their post list

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def add_post(self, post):
        self.posts[post.author_id].append(post)  # record a post

    def _already_related(self, user_id_a, user_id_b):
        if user_id_b in self.users[user_id_a].connections:  # already connected
            return True
        for r in self.requests.values():  # scan existing requests
            same_pair = (r.from_user_id == user_id_a and r.to_user_id == user_id_b) or \
                        (r.from_user_id == user_id_b and r.to_user_id == user_id_a)
            if same_pair and r.status == RequestStatus.PENDING:  # a pending request already exists
                return True
        return False  # no existing relationship or pending request

    def send_connection_request(self, from_user_id, to_user_id, factory):
        if self._already_related(from_user_id, to_user_id):  # already connected or already pending
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_duplicate_request_rejected(from_user_id, to_user_id)  # notify
            raise DuplicateConnectionException(f"A request or connection already exists between {from_user_id} and {to_user_id}")
        request = factory.create_request(from_user_id, to_user_id)  # build request
        self.requests[request.request_id] = request                  # store it
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_connection_request_sent(request)  # notify
        return request  # hand back to caller

    def respond_to_request(self, request_id, accept):
        request = self.requests.get(request_id)  # look up request
        if request is None:
            raise InvalidRequestException(f"Unknown request: {request_id}")
        if request.status != RequestStatus.PENDING:  # already resolved
            raise RequestAlreadyRespondedException(f"Request {request_id} was already responded to")
        if accept:  # recipient accepts
            request.status = RequestStatus.ACCEPTED  # mark accepted
            self.users[request.from_user_id].connections.add(request.to_user_id)  # edge, sender side
            self.users[request.to_user_id].connections.add(request.from_user_id)  # edge, recipient side
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_connection_accepted(request)  # notify
        else:  # recipient rejects
            request.status = RequestStatus.REJECTED  # mark rejected, no edge
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_connection_rejected(request)  # notify

    def get_connection_degree(self, user_id_a, user_id_b):
        if user_id_a == user_id_b:
            return 0  # same user, degree zero
        visited = {user_id_a}     # nodes already explored
        queue = [user_id_a]         # BFS frontier
        depth = {user_id_a: 0}       # distance from user_id_a
        head = 0                      # index-based queue pointer
        while head < len(queue):        # explore level by level
            current = queue[head]         # next node
            head += 1
            current_depth = depth[current]  # its distance
            if current_depth >= 3:            # do not expand past the cap
                continue
            for neighbor in self.users[current].connections:  # scan its connections
                if neighbor == user_id_b:
                    return current_depth + 1  # found the target
                if neighbor not in visited:     # first time seeing it
                    visited.add(neighbor)
                    depth[neighbor] = current_depth + 1
                    queue.append(neighbor)
        return 4  # not found within 3 hops: reported as "beyond 3rd degree"

    def generate_feed(self, user_id):
        candidates = []  # gathered posts
        for connection_id in self.users[user_id].connections:  # scan direct connections only
            candidates.extend(self.posts[connection_id])          # include all their posts
        return self.ranking_strategy.rank(candidates)  # delegate ordering to the strategy

items: Why cap BFS at 3 hops instead of computing the exact degree? Real professional networks summarize anything beyond 3rd-degree as a single bucket for both privacy and performance reasons; capping the search reflects that product decision directly in the algorithm.

Why check for an existing pending request in both directions rather than just fromUserId to toUserId? Because a request from Bob to Alice should block Alice from also sending one to Bob; the relationship is symmetric even before it is accepted.

How would this BFS approach scale to hundreds of millions of users? It would not, as an in-memory adjacency map; production systems back this with a graph database or a precomputed, periodically refreshed shortest-path index.

Live BFS per query vs precomputed degree index: live BFS is always accurate and simple to implement, at the cost of repeated traversal cost per query; a precomputed index trades staleness for speed at scale.

1st-degree-only feed vs including 2nd-degree: 1st-degree-only is simple and predictable, at the cost of a sparser feed for users with few connections; including 2nd-degree content requires careful ranking to avoid noise.

Symmetric undirected connections vs asymmetric "following": undirected connections model mutual professional relationships well, but a platform wanting one-way content subscription (like following a company page) would need a separate, directed relationship type alongside this one.
Persist users, requests, connections, and posts in a database rather than in-memory maps, using the schema in the Database Design section.

Emit request/connection/post events to a message queue so downstream systems (notifications, feed pre-computation, search indexing) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Add idempotency keys to sendConnectionRequest so retried network requests cannot create duplicate requests.
Precompute and cache feed results per user, invalidating on new posts from their connections, rather than recomputing on every read.
